speakeroldname: Mr. R. J. Orange (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: HUNDREDTH BIRTHDAY OF ESTABLISHMENT AS PART OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. At the time of Confederation, Canada included only Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and a very small portion of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Between the tiny Canada of that day in the east and British Columbia in the west stretched the vast, undeveloped, largely unexplored and sparsely populated lands owned by the Hudson's Bay Company.
In 1868 the Rupert's Land Act by the British Imperial Parliament authorized the purchase by the Dominion of Canada of the immense tracts of land known as Rupert's Land and the Northwestern Territory. One hundred years ago today, on June 23, 1870, Queen Victoria signed the order which transferred these lands to the government of Canada and which granted to the Parliament of Canada authority to legislate for their future welfare and good government upon the terms and conditions therein stated.
Thus Canada grew from a small country huddled along the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence River and the Atlantic seaboard to a mighty nation stretching north to the Arctic Ocean and west to the Pacific. The people of the Northwest Territories are Canadians first, proud of their contribution to our nation, its heritage and its culture.
The riches of the Canadian north, both of its people and of its resources, offer to Canada a unique opportunity to develop a truly Canadian identity from the Atlantic to the Arctic to the Pacific, from sea to sea to sea.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CENTRAL DEPOSITORY FOR SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement to the House concerning the creation of a central depository for securities in Canada. For a few years now, some prominent Canadian financial and investment institutions have been considering the feasibility of establishing such a central depository. This led very recently to the incorporation under Part I of the Canada Corporations Act of the Canadian Depository for Securities Limited.
This corporation is a non-profit, service venture with no public financial involvement; most of the major financial and investment institutions are committed to its eventual operation.
The purpose of the depository is to facilitate the transfer of shares across Canada by computerized bookkeeping entries, thereby reducing the need for physical transfer of share certificates and the attendant administrative problems and costs.
Incorporation of this company under the Canada Corporations Act is an interim step. Before it can begin to operate as a depository it will require special powers now reserved for trust companies and not granted to companies incorporated under the Canada Corporations Act. It will also require government supervision in order to maintain full confidence in the system.
For these reasons, and in view of the fact that the creation of the depository will be an important forward step in the operation of the Canadian securities market, the government intends to present to Parliament in due course legislation which would give the depository the special powers needed for its effective operation.
For the further information of the House, I should like to table a letter I have written to the corporation's solicitor, outlining the government's position and intention in this matter.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CENTRAL DEPOSITORY FOR SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having had an opportunity to consider this matter as a result of the minister having sent me notice of his intention to make this statement, I should like to make a few comments. I think this is a step in the right direction, albeit there would have been much more progress if it had been wedded to

a similar indication of progress on the establishment of a Canadian securities commission. The central depository for securities is a cooperative venture made possible through amendments to the Canada Corporations Act. It is important to determine where the location of this depository shall be. That is a matter that could be settled through co-operation with the provinces. The federal government and the provinces should agree upon the ultimate location of the securities commission and also agree upon the location of this depository because the two go hand in hand.
I agree with the minister that there will be a sensible reduction in the loss of time and in expense. The method of supervision has not been indicated but I hope it will come under the Superintendent of Insurance rather than under some other body.
Under these circumstances I think it is a welcome announcement. We look forward to this matter having high priority at the opening of the new session as far as legislative changes are concerned and we hope that it will not have to wait for the abolition of symbols in other places.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF CENTRAL DEPOSITORY FOR SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this age of computers a central depository for securities is a necessity and we are therefore pleased to see that such an organization is to be established. Since the purpose is to ease the physical transfer of shares and other assets, I question why it is being brought in as a corporation involving the financial institutions. In view of the fact that the minister has stated it will require government supervision to maintain full confidence in the system, it would seem that the logical and uncomplicated thing to do would be to set it up as a Crown corporation somewhat similar to the Bank of Canada or a land registry office where a fee would be charged for the use of the service. There is no explanation why it was not done in that way.
We may find ourselves following the same path as we did with the Bank of Canada when an attempt was made to set it up as an instrument in which the financial institutions would play a role. It was discovered that it would not work this way and would have to act as an instrument of public policy. It seems to me, barring some explanation, that this is not the sensible way to set up this organization and that the minister should seriously consider the establishment of a Crown corporation. Desirable as the purpose is, I think it is frustrated by the manner in which he proposes to set up this body.
June 23, 1970

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the House I should like to make a statement about the conclusions which the government has reached with respect to the recommendations of Volume III of the report of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bicul-turalism. As hon. members will be aware, this volume deals with "The Work World", including the public service and armed forces as well as the private sector.
I am pleased to state that the government is able to accept in principle the broad objectives proposed for the public service by the Royal Commission. The general lines of these objectives are that the French language should increasingly become a language of work in the public service, that the atmosphere of the public service should represent the lingustic and cultural reality of Canadian society, and that Canadians whose mother tongue is French should be adequately represented in the public service-both in terms of numbers and in levels of responsibility.
The fifty-seven recommendations which Volume III of the report sets forth have been the subject of detailed study by a committee of senior officials and have been given careful consideration by ministers. The suggestions put forward by the Commission involve far-reaching changes in some instances, and they have been given the close attention which they deserve.

I wish to table, with the consent of the House, a detailed document which outlines the existing management objectives in this field and comments on the recommendations made by the commission. I have two copies in both official languages, Mr. Speaker.

The fundamental consideration to which I am sure all Canadians fully subscribe is one of equality of opportunity in
Bilingualism and Biculturalism the words of the commission's report, "a real equality of opportunity, ensuring that the fact of speaking English or French would be neither a help nor a handicap to a person seeking entry into the institutions affecting our individual and collective life."
In the Federal Public Service, equal opportunity is closely related to the merit principle which cannot be said to be fully operative unless it extends to qualified francophones with little or no knowledge of English a recognition equal to that which it accords anglophones whose knowledge of French is similarly limited. I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that we in no sense propose to limit the merit principle, but rather to fulfil it.
At this point I might put it to the House that, this general principle having been stated, if we want to get on faster I could table the rest of my statement which has been distributed to the leaders of the parties.

As the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) says, I need the practice. I am not quite sure if that practice could ever improve my performance. However, I am perfectly happy to take the time of the House to read on as suggested by the Conservative party.

The recommendations of the Commission can be considered under five main headings:
First, general principles. The first group of recommendations deals with the general principles of Public Service organization and management. It includes three recommendations (Nos. 1, 2 and 5) concerning the establishment of French-language units, and two more (Nos. 3 and 4) dealing with the appointment of francophones to the most senior positions in the public service.
There has, I think, been a great deal of misunderstanding about the notion of French-language units. I stated some time ago that we could not accept the creation of ghettos in which French-Canadian public servants would be divided off from their English-Canadian colleagues. Of course, this was not the Commissioners' intention.
June 23. 1970

Bilingualism, and Biculturalism
Their comments make it clear that they had in mind units in which the main language of work would be French, but which could include both anglophone and francophone public servants. In our opinion, what the Royal Commission hoped to see accomplished was simply an extension of measures which it had already recommended to make the Public Service a bilingual institution. Viewed in that way, French-language units could have several advantages: for example, they would permit the recruitment and participation of unilingual francophones on a more equal footing with unilingual anglophones. By the same token, this procedure would open the way to a greater reliance on a manpower source that has not until now been adequately used, that is, those well-qualified francophone candidates whose knowledge of English is limited. It is a pool of talent from which the federal Public Service has been largely cut off. At the same time, the French language units would provide a milieu in which anglophone public servants who have invested great effort in acquiring second language skills would have the opportunity of becoming fluent in the French language, just as many of their francophone colleagues are now fluent in the English language. Such units would operate in favour of a greater degree of individual bilingualism at senior levels of the Public Service. They should also make it easier for French to take its place with English as a language of work in the federal administration.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)

The upshot of this, in the government's view, is that French language units should be considered as a means to an end, a useful tool in helping to advance toward a bilingual public service. Indeed, a number of francophone units, or units which come close to what the commissioners had in mind, are already in operation in the Federal Public Service in Quebec, in the Armed Forces and in some departments in Ottawa where they appear to work effectively and without difficulty.
It is clear that the consequence of establishing such units cannot be judged in the abstract. The government therefore believes that in an initial period they should be set up on an experimental basis which would permit a better informed decision to be taken at a later date as to whether the system can be viable in the long term. The application of

the use of French would be established progressively in these French language units so that during a preliminary period, as an aid to anglophone participants in such units, the choice of language for written work would be optional.
On the understanding, then, that the units should not be considered an end in themselves, and that we should have an open and experimental attitude toward their potential advantages and disadvantages, we are prepared to go ahead over the next year or so with pilot projects in a number of departments designed to test this idea more fully.
We are also inclined to believe, Mr. Speaker, that there has been some misunderstanding concerning the Royal Commission's recommendations on the appointment of francophones to the Public Service and government task forces. I should make it clear that the government has no difficulty whatever in accepting recommendation No. 4 to the effect that federal planning and advisory bodies, task forces and similar groups should include "effectively balanced participation by Anglophones and Francophones". This is already government policy and has been for some time. Nor do we find it difficult to agree that such balanced participation should also be an important consideration in the appointment of senior officials. I must emphasize, however, that we do not accept that this in any way represents a modification of the merit principle. The first requirement will always be to search for the public servant who best merits the job. We see no inconsistency in ensuring the maintenance of this principle and at the same time respecting the need for full participation in the Federal Public Service by members of both the Anglophone and Francophone communities.

Second, the language policy. The next group of recommendations (Nos. 6 to 15 and No. 21) deals in some detail with language policy in the public service, in relation to recruitment, training and the work situation. In large measure these recommendations are straightforward in nature and can be accepted without difficulty; in fact a number of them have been reflected in government policy for some time. Although we recognize that a great deal remains to be done in this area, I am pleased to say that considerable progress has already been made toward realizing the objectives which are set by these recommendations.
June 23. 1970

Third, the public service organization. The next series of recommendations includes a number of suggestions regarding recruitment, promotion, and conditions of' employment (recommendations 16 to 20), as well as suggestions with respect to organizational changes relating to the implementation of the recommendations put forward in Volume III, recommendations 22 to 24.
In general these recommendations are acceptable to the government, but I would like to draw the attention of the House to three in particular.
With regard to Recommendation 17, the government is of course prepared to recruit qualified persons abroad, whether in Englishspeaking countries or French-speaking countries, but only after it has been demonstrated that Canadian sources have been examined and that no qualified Canadians are available. This requirement is included in the Public Service Employment Act, and the government sees no reason to propose that it be altered.
The government has given careful consideration to the Commission's recommendation 22 that a new Public Service Authority be established. A number of developments have taken place in this field since the Commissioners carried out their study, and these have had a considerable bearing on our analysis of this proposal. In particular, a new service was established in the Secretary of State Department in 1969, whose responsibility it is to co-ordinate the implementation of the government's official languages policy. In order to avoid waste and duplication, we consider it more rational to maintain and reinforce this organization rather than to establish a new bureau with responsibilities in the same field. We are convinced that by proceeding in this way we will reduce administrative delays and speed up progress towards bilingualism in the public service.

Fourth, the armed forces. The next group of recommendations, numbers 25 to 41, relates to the Canadian Armed Forces. They have been the subject of detailed study in consultation with the military authorities, and I am happy to be able to say that, on the whole, the Armed Forces are already working in the directions indicated by these recommendations. Nevertheless, although they are acceptable to the government it would be misleading to suggest that the measures recommended in this field by the commissioners can be accomplished overnight or without
Bilingualism and Biculturalism difficulty. Changes of this magnitude require considerable effort and can only be introduced gradually if standards of efficiency and morale are to be maintained.
Fifth, the private sector. On the whole, the recommendations in this section are not addressed to the federal government. I might say, however, that we understand the reasons which led the commissioners to make a number of recommendations concerning the private sector, for a bilingual Canada cannot be achieved if efforts are restricted to governmental activities alone. We recognize, moreover, that the situation in the past has not been satisfactory and we believe Canadians will agree that changes are needed. Indeed, certain private firms and institutions have already shown what it is possible to accomplish with good will and a determined effort. Those responsible are to be commended, in my view, for having acted on their own initiative and I hope that increasing numbers of private institutions will see the need for further steps in this direction. For its part the government will be pleased to do whatever it can to encourage and assist them.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
The proposals which the commissioners have put forward to establish task forces involving government, business, labour and universities seem to us to be reasonable. Although they are not addressed to the federal government as such, I can assure the provincial authorities that we will be pleased to play a part in this process if that is their wish. Moreover, in so far as recommendation 42 is addressed to the federal government, we are certainly prepared to ensure that the French language is used in our operations in all appropriate circumstances. We also have no hesitation in accepting two of the recommendations in this series, numbers 56 and 57, which are directly addressed to the federal government.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we must recognize in all honesty that the effort to move toward a bilingual country is one to which Canadians have come very late in the day. As a result, we do not expect that the goal will be reached overnight; nor do we expect it will be easy to accomplish. We believe, however, and we think that this view is confirmed by discussions with provincial governments, groups and individuals across the country, that there is a new attitude toward bilingualism in Canada and a willingness to work towards its realization. We con-
June 23, 1970

Bilingualism and Biculturalism sider that the recommendations contained in Book III should be seen in this light, as a part of an ongoing effort which cannot be imposed on a people, but which will grow out of a sense of co-operation, mutual respect and understanding. Mr. Speaker, it is my profound hope that all Canadians will wish to join in making these ideals a reality. That is all I have to read at this time, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must begin by expressing admiration for the obvious reluctance of the Prime Minister, (Mr. Trudeau) to take very much of the time of the House to make this statement, particularly in view of the special significance of tomorrow. I do wish to thank him for sending me a copy of his statement with the attached papers this morning.
This is obviously a subject of great importance, a subject of great sensitivity and a subject in respect of which we would obviously wish to weigh our words carefully and also speak quite frankly. This is a very far-reaching statement by the Prime Minister with very far-reaching implications. I think I can summarize his statement by saying that generally speaking he is accepting the recommendations of the commission in the third volume, with one very important exception.
Let me refer to recommendation No. 22 which will be found on page 8 of the document tabled by the Prime Minister. The commissioners say:
We recommend the creation of a Public Service Language Authority. This new body will be responsible for a) planning, implementing, and maintaining institutional bilingualism-
This recommendation was not accepted by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister instead said the government had decided to amplify and develop a service that had been established in the Department of the Secretary of State. In other words, instead of establishing the formal authority recommended by the commission, presumably by Act of Parliament, the Prime Minister and the government have chosen to utilize a service within the Department of the Secretary of State.
This is of vital importance. What are the terms of reference of the Secretary of State's authority? What are his terms of reference in regard to exercising the control he will presumably exercise over every other department of government and the Armed Forces

within, of course, the terms of reference? What are the terms of reference of his authority with regard to the private sector?
The government itself has great power to influence private institutions and private companies in this country. It is no exaggeration to say that the tentacles of the federal government are everywhere. Precisely what is the Secretary of State going to do to "encourage and assist private institutions" to take further steps toward bilingualism? We do not know.
I do not propose to commit myself or my party at this time to the establishment of a public service language authority, but at least such an authority would be set up by Act of Parliament and would give Parliament and the country an opportunity to discuss these matters. Certainly I have no hesitation in condemning as strongly as I can the tactic of the government to avoid this kind of discussion by giving this kind of authority to a service in the Secretary of State's department with undefined terms of reference.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONCLUSIONS OF GOVERNMENT WITH RESPECT TO VOLUME III OF COMMISSION'S REPORT

I suggest that this is a far-reaching matter. It is a matter that ought to be discussed in Parliament. It is a matter that ought to be discussed in Parliament in such a way that the public which wishes to express its views could do so to a committee of the House. This could have been done if the recommendation of the commission had been followed and a bill introduced, for example, to establish a public service language authority. Nobody in the House would disagree that this is of special importance. At least in this way it would bring the matter before the House in a manner presumably in line with the views of the commission. The Prime Minister is avoiding this.
What are the Secretary of State's terms of reference? We may be told they are contained in the recommendations included in the third volume of the B and B commission report. If these are the terms of reference they could be changed presumably any day by cabinet minute.
I think we have to recognize that relations between linguistic groups are always somewhat difficult. There is always a certain amount of fear and suspicion, whether or not it is justified. Therefore it is most important that we avoid this as much as possible. It is very important that we establish institutions and that we take steps in such a way so as to
June 23, 1970

reduce to a minimum the possibilities of fear and suspicion as to what may be going on.
The Prime Minister wants to use the Department of the Secretary of State as a vehicle "to speed up progress towards bilingualism in the Public Service". That is the Prime Minister's aim. In choosing this vehicle he may actually set it back. The old adage of more haste, less speed, may be appropriate here, because this is a very far-reaching step being taken, as I say, with no real public discussion. The measures are subject to no real public control or knowledge because they are being relegated, as I judge the Prime Minister's statement, to the secret recesses of the government.
I have in the past expressed concern about the concept of unilingual working units. I suggested that this is a backward step and to that extent an abandonment of the concept of bilingualism. I referred to the danger that we might develop some new solitudes. This is still my belief.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
Are we to proceed without more discussion than we are having here this afternoon? Are we merely to have this brief exchange? The Prime Minister joked about the length of his statement. Are we to have this relatively brief discussion and then turn everything over to the Department of the Secretary of State to administer from now on?
The Prime Minister referred to the question of senior appointments and the merit system. He said that the merit system would not be modified in any way by an attempt to balance senior appointments in terms of language. There may be very good reason to balance senior appointments in terms of language, but it is nonsense to pretend that this would not be a modification of the merit system. We would be modifying the merit system if we were to adopt a system whereby so many senior appointments would come from each region. There might be reason for this, but it would be a1 modification of the merit system. So I do not think the Prime Minister should stand up in the House and say that this is not a modification of the merit system. It may very well be defensible, but it is a modification of the merit system.
I say again that it is wrong to proceed in this way. This is the same way Information Canada was set up. It was set up by government decree. This is a further concentration of power. I suggest it is an abuse of power and is an excessive resort to secrecy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
I say again that the commission itself recommended a procedure that would be open and that would call for the government coming before the House and the country to present its measures and persuade the country to adopt those measures. But even had the commission not made that recommendation I would still believe that Parliament and the people of this country should have an opportunity to discuss these matters and make their views known before the policy is settled and shunted off once and for all to be administered by a department of government.
I wish to emphasize that I do not say this because the present Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) is a French-speaking Canadian. The situation might be more serious and a little more under suspicion if he were an Englishspeaking Canadian. The principle, however, is the same. We are faced not only with a fait accompli but with the administration of this policy in the future and with the development of this policy in the future being conducted within the secrecy of the cabinet and administered by departmental decisions.
I say in all seriousness that the government is creating an atmosphere which will encourage suspicion to flourish. I do not like that. I do not like it a bit, and I ask the government to reconsider more earnestly the manner in which it is proceeding and its intention apparently to deal with this simply as another departmental operation. I ask most sincerely, in fact I insist, that the government proceed in such a manner that this matter can come before the House and be discussed in such a way that interested Canadians will have an opportunity to make their views known.

I remind the House that it was only as late as 1966, indeed on April 6, 1966, that the then Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Lester Pearson, made a statement with regard to bilingualism in the federal service. Indeed, Book III of the commission's report reproduces that statement as one of the appendices. At that time, speaking for my party, I said that it is a measure of the insensitivity by which we have treated our country and the language question that it was not until the 99th year of the existence of Confederation that the Prime Minister of Canada produced a co-ordinated statement about bilingual policy in the federal service. It is a measure also of the neglect of 100 years that it was not until the 103rd year of Confederation that the policy merely started by the right hon. Mr. Pearson in 1966 received fuller implementation in the statement we had today. As one Canadian I know the immense harm this failure to recognize the bilingual character of Canada inside the federal civil service has done to the unity of the country. I express with the Prime Minister and every other Canadian the sincere hope that these steps are not too late.
I am also very glad that the Prime Minister and the government have decided to deal with the French language units on an experimental basis. When I first read Book III of the commission's report I wondered whether the commissioners are not being a little too theoretical rather than practical in their propositions, because it is important that we not create language ghettos in the federal public service and not create a situation where one language unit competes with another language unit, whether of the same language or of the second official language, which is likely to be the case. Furthermore, it would seem to me that these things must not be artificially imposed. They ought to be developed functionally, to use a favourite word of the Prime Minister, as the situation makes it natural that the language unit be developed in a given department, Crown corporation or agency. Therefore, on behalf of my colleagues and myself I welcome the fact that the government intends to proceed step by step with these units as a pilot project in order to study the advantages and disadvantages before any large-scale work is done in this field.
I remind hon. members, and I think it is important to emphasize it, that when we speak of Anglophones in Canada we are not

What is involved is the maintenance of a high quality of civil servants in the civil service, and the matter of language should be used as an instrument for improving that quality and never be allowed, because of pressures, to reduce the quality in our federal civil service in order to satisfy either one or other of the main language groups in this country. It could become an agency unto its own end, as it were. Instead

Having said that, I express on behalf of my colleagues and myself entire agreement with the statement of the Leader of the Opposition in criticism of the government for putting this into the Department of the Secretary of State, without telling us exactly what it is that they are putting there. I suggest it is the Prime Minister's duty, as a part of governmental organization, to set up in the Secretary of State's Department a separate division having to do with language, for which there should be a separate vote in the estimates, for which there ought to be regular reports to Parliament on which the minister and his officials can be regularly questioned, and on which their work can receive the scrutiny and, if necessary, the criticism of Members of Parliament and of the public.
It is totally inadequate to say that his department is doing this. I want to know who is doing this. Who is the person, who are the people, what is the division, who is the head of it, what policies are they pursuing, what are they trying to accomplish, and what are their objectives? subtopic: CONCLUSIONS OF GOVERNMENT WITH RESPECT TO VOLUME III OF COMMISSION'S REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the general agreement which the government is in a position to give to the main objectives set forth by the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism in volume III of its report must not let us overlook the fact that the national problem is of such far-reaching consequences that a mere agreement in principle is far from satisfactory.
At a time when 650,000 Quebecers decide in favour of a provincial party advocating Quebec independence, it is rather strange to note to what extent the Prime Minister soft-pedals the essential recommendations of the Commission. What may appear as radical and drastic solutions to an English-speaking Canadian is merely basic justice to a Frenchspeaking Canadian.
The Prime Minister states, and I quote:
In the Federal Public Service, equal opportunity is closely related to the merit principle-
-I emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that we in no sense propose to limit the merit principle, but rather to fulfill it.
Saying this, he seems to ignore an actual situation which makes the knowledge of English an essential requirement of the merit system he referred to. One only has to try to get in touch with senior officials in various federal departments to find out that it is still very difficult to obtain information or to carry on discussions in French with them.
Some progress has indeed been made. But much more will be needed in order to achieve the true equality we all hope for. I would like to emphasize a particular paragraph of the Prime Minister's statement which puzzles me. At page 3 of his statement, he says, and I quote:
The application of the use of French would be established progressively in these French-language units so that during a preliminary period, as an aid to anglophone participants in such units, the choice of language for written work would be optional.
We do not object to helping anglophone participants to learn French, but if French units are designed for that purpose alone, nothing will change. The fire that burns brightly at night on St. Jean Baptiste Day will slowly go out. And the Prime Minister's good intentions, on the eve of French Canada's national day, will come to nothing in the English bureaucracy.

As I said, I welcome the Prime Minister's statement but I am afraid that it is not forceful enough.
While in Quebec we have put behind us forever the little "Baptiste" with his blond curls and even the tall "Baptiste", in Ottawa the sheep is shyly coming in.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the House rose on Monday, June 22, clause 13 was under consideration with an amendment by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra which reads as follows:
That clause 13 be amended by striking out line 26 on page 23 and substituting the following: "at least 50 of the electoral districts of Canada."
On Clause 13, subclause 8-Deletions from Registry.

Mr. Chairman, when I moved this amendment at the previous sitting an amendment has been moved earlier that this number be set at 25. This is a case of finding something that is agreeable to the members and which will fit. One could say that a party of 75 would be too large, particularly when one thinks of the maritime provinces or the Prairies as a whole. One might think that this number is too small when one thinks in terms of a federal party within this House. We must compromise in order to arrive at the right figure. It is not really so much a matter of argument as a matter of taste. It is like Goldilocks seeking the right bowl of porridge, one will be too hot and another too cold. Some figure will perhaps be just right, and I suggested 50 in my amendment.

Mr. Chairman, before I refer specifically to the amendment, let me say I had a discussion a few minutes ago with the House Leader in reference to subsection (b) part 1 of the original Act where the word "and" appears. It seems to me that with the interpretation that has been put on this section that "and" should be "or".
As I read the Act now, the fact that a party or a purported party had no representation in the House of Commons would mean it would 22478-482
Canada Elections Act
be excluded from having a party label on the ballot. From the discussions that have gone on within our caucus and, as I understand it among government members as well, this was clearly not the intent of that section. I hope this matter will be clarified very early this afternoon.
Referring specifically to the amendment, the hon. member who preceded me suggested that his proposal to alter the number of candidates to be nominated in order that a party label be attached to a person's name on the ballot, being reduced from 75 to 50, represents some kind of compromise which should be accepted. This seems to be not the type of item in respect of which we should have a compromise. There is a basic democratic right at issue here.
In any legislative matter it is sensible, and indeed desirable, in any meaningful sense of politics to bring about compromises. One may argue at a given time that a minimum wage of $2 is appropriate. This depends on the economic and political conditions. It may make sense to effect a compromise in reaching a final decision. When we are considering the proposal to recognize the right of political parties to appear by name on ballots, it seems to me we are not dealing with a type of item that should be considered in terms of compromise.
It has been recognized for a long time in our political system, since early in the last century, that wherever there is a democratic system in a modern industrial age at least there are bound to be political parties. One of the anachronisms in our society in Canada, and elsewhere, is that political parties have obtained almost no official recognition in terms of the law. One distinct advantage in terms of democracy in respect of this bill we have before us is that it does intend to give legal recognition to the existence of political parties. I believe there would be an important weakness in this bill if it did not recognize the right of any man or small group of individuals to start a new political party and present a program to the electorate, whether in one municipality, in one province or on the basis of a national appeal. The real issue is that party politics is an integral part of our democratic system. Therefore, I do not think we should weigh the electoral system against the emergence of new political and social changes in this country, no matter how insignificantly these might be regarded by the rest of us at the outset.

June 23, 1970
Canada Elections Act
One thing we should all have learned by now, as a result of the history of the last 100 years, is that new political parties and new movements constantly occur in society. Therefore, I object to the principle of compromise on this issue and would like to see the whole of subsection 2 struck out. I do not propose any specific wording at this point. We will get around to that later. It would seem to me that the principle we should recognize in respect of this legislation is the right of one man or two men to begin a political party, obtain nomination through the correct procedure and, following that, have their name and their party listed on the ballot.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
While there is a difference of opinion between the hon. member and myself on this question, I think he will recognize that there is also a difference of opinion between himself and his colleague the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre on this point. As I understood the amendment of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre he wished to reduce the threshold to 27 candidates. The bill states 75 candidates and the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra proposes what is close to the arithmetical mean of 50 candidates. In my view of the matter 50 candidates would still achieve the objective the government had in mind without being so restrictive as the requirement of 75 candidates 28 days before polling day. Therefore, I would be inclined to accept the amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra.
In respect of the other point, I would accept the view that subclause 8 of clause 13 does require a careful reading, but my opinion, confirmed by talking to the draftsman, is that this would not have the effect, as the hon. member would seem to fear, of excluding his group from being able to become registered. In effect these are cumulative criteria which will be operative after the twenty-eighth day.
We are talking about a group not previously recognized in this House which did not have 75, 50 or any number of candidates in the field. In essence, there are two criteria in respect of a description of a group. There might be some argument that if it was changed to "or" the hon. member's group might be excluded, but I do not quite see that particular argument. The way I read it, I think a fair interpretation of the matter, is that here we are talking about a political grouping which in the first place is not represented in the House of Commons and which in the second place did not nominate 50 can-

didates in the field on the 28th day before election. Therefore, I think it is properly "and" rather than the disjunctive "or" in the circumstances. In the circumstances, I believe the clause is quite correct as it stands.

Mr. Chairman, I am beginning to feel that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby had a point. Do I understand that a political party which had no members in this House only need have the number of candidates specified in clause (b)(ii)? Is that the intent?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. The chief Electoral Officer has no authority to delete any such grouping unless these two criteria are not met.

I am impressed, Mr. Chairman, at the rather breezy and easy way in which we are playing the numbers game. Surely, there is something more serious to this than striking an arithmetical means. The government decided not to accept the recommendation of the committee that the number should be 26. The government chose 75. Surely, some thought must have been given to that. The suggestion that the number 50 is the mean point is interesting mathematically, but surely there must have been some more thought given to this than merely picking the number out of one's head.
I would have thought that the minister whose government saw fit to change the committee's recommendations might have defended the change by giving us some reason for it, so that we would be prone to listen carefully and weigh it. If this becomes law, we are introducing the suggestion that we would not countenance a group of people being independent of, or splinters of, the various parties. It would seem to me that if we are talking about a national party there should be some reason for hitting upon a number which would reflect a potential natural expression through the political process. I should like to know the special virtue of the number 50. The fact that it lies between 26 and 75 does not impress me.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is nothing more fundamental behind the choice of 50 than the committee's choice of 26 or 27. Really, what is involved is a difference of opinion concerning what a substantial political grouping should be in order to achieve recognition under our electoral law. I did take the point made by several of my colleagues on this side of the House that 75 is
June 23, 1970

obviously very much tougher to achieve on the 28th day before election than 50. There is no magic in the figure, any more than there is in respect of the voting age. I am prepared to accept it as a suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the House Leader would deal with the point I tried to make that this is not the type of issue in respect of which we should try to effect a compromise, and that, in the fundamental interests of a parliamentary democracy, our electoral laws should recognize a man or a few men as constituting a political party. I cannot see any practical objection to linking the name of the party with the candidate's name. The principal argument suggests the contrary. Would the House Leader address himself to that?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should perhaps say that the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre seems to have been persuaded by the same argument I was. We may both be wrong, but I make the point that we are talking about national political parties and would want some expression of a very substantial political position by having the candidates nominated and put into the field.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I acknowledge that 75 was too tough. I would be prepared to lower the threshold. On the other hand, I think 27 is too low. That was the basic proposition to which the committee agreed, and apparently the hon. member does not agree with that.

Mr. Chairman, I think we should correct one misunderstanding on the part of the President of the Privy Council, perhaps not a misunderstanding but an attempt to be divisive. There is no basic difference between the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, myself and others in the NDP, and the position taken by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. All the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre was doing was trying to indicate that the Standing Committee had made the determination of 10 per cent. That was a unanimous decision of the Standing Committee.
Obviously, the President of the Privy Council and the government were not content to accept the unanimous view of the committee, agreed to by the Liberal members on that committee, and so came in with the counter proposal of 75, which is far above 10 per cent of the number of members in this House. The
Canada Elections Act
hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre chose the number 27 as the next highest whole number over 10 per cent of the membership of the House. In fact, 10 per cent would be 26.4 members. I will admit that there are a number of members on the opposite side of the chamber who would qualify to be placed in the .4 position. However, we wanted the next whole number, and that is why 27 was chosen, to represent the unanimous view of the committee.
Within the Standing Committee, we argued that it should not be the prerogative of one political group to make any determination about what should constitute another political group. We put forward that argument a number of years ago when a decision was pending as to where the Raillement de Credi-tiste, or Social Credit party as it then was, would sit in the House, and whether a party should have 12 members in the House before its leader could receive the additional remuneration set aside for party leaders. We have constantly advanced the argument that basically it is wrong for political groups to impose restrictions on other political groups, some of which may not have yet come into existence. Apparently the President of the Privy Council is not content to accept the sage advice of the Liberal members of the Standing Committee.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder who is being partisan now. I would point out that I just turned the logic of the hon. member for Skeena against his colleague, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. The latter does not accept the fact that the threshold has to be set. He does not accept the argument of the hon. member for Skeena and asserts that one, three or five individuals running as candidates should be able to claim all the privileges of a political party. That is all I am pointing out to the hon. member for Skeena and to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre who, in pressing the amendment last night providing for the number 27, accepted the principle that a threshold has to be set somewhere in order to determine what will be a national political party. I doubt very much that I can satisfy the hon. member for Skeena, but I think this amendment is acceptable to a large number of hon. members, including members of the Standing Committee.

Mr. Chairman, we should always look for a middle course. The motion proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver

June 23, 1970
Canada Elections Act
Quadra (Mr. Deachman) is acceptable because it provides that to get official recognition in an election, a party must have at least 50 candidates.
It is essential to determine a reasonable figure, neither too high nor too low, because it would not be fair to require of a new party to have 264 candidates in an election in order to be considered officially.
However, since only national parties are recognized, 50 is an acceptable figure and we support the motion.

Mr. Chairman, at meetings of the Standing Committee, hon. members expressed preferences varying from zero to something over 100, with respect to the number of candidates who should run in order for a group to be qualified as a political party. My own personal opinion is that the reality of the situation demands that we have a party system in Canada. I guess I can be called a party person in more ways than one, and while people have a perfect right to form a political party and run candidates, I have always resented the frivolity that we have seen the odd time in Canadian history. On one occasion a group called the Rhinoceros Party ran candidates, in either a provincial or federal election. I think that was nothing more than an attempt to demean our electoral process. If people disagree with the kind of process we have, I say they had better be damned serious about opposing it. They should be serious about political parties. This is why I, personally, felt the figure of 10 per cent of the membership of the House would be fair.
I feel that the threshold, as the President of the Privy Council calls it, should be as low as possible. I can still see nothing good about the amendment that is before us. It is perhaps better than the government proposal, but it is not as good as the one I moved. As the hon. member for Skeena said, I moved my amendment merely to make an honest women out of the government, by calling on it to implement the committee's recommendation. The Standing Committee attempted to come up with an unanimous recommendation. After hearing all the arguments we agreed on 10 per cent of the membership of the House. That did not mean all of us liked that, but we agreed to it. If the President of the Privy Council could come down a little lower than the number 50, he would make some hon. members on both sides of the chamber much happier.
[Mr. Beaudoin.l
Mr. Chairman, in this party we don't play politics.
Oh, oh.
I just want to say I am always sorry when a carefully thought out recommendation of a committee is callously and casually brushed aside by the government.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then, why did you move an amendment yesterday?

I am not impressed with the non-argument of the mover of this amendment. I do insist, however, despite the logic of the presentation of the hon. members to my left, that there is a point in pragmatic judgment where the state, if it is going to recognize parties, can surely say that a group with one candidate is not a national party. So, there is some basis for making a numerical decision, and because 50 is better than 75 I am going to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. I hope that this will carry so that we can move on, because I have no desire to spend the first half of the month of July on this legislation.

eliminate the requirement that a deposit of $200 be posted by a candidate in a general election. I am proposing my amendment because I believe it to be wrong that a person or political party should be exposed to potential financial loss as a result of participation in our democratic process. Probably the basis of the requirement of a deposit, if we were to look at its historical genesis, is that people wanted to prevent the proliferation of political parties. I think that there are sufficient guarantees against that kind of proliferation of political parties in Canada. The first guarantee which militates against the establishment of a large number of parties and the fragmentation of the representation in parliament is the existence of single member constituencies. The second factor which militates against the fragmentation of the party system in the country is the solidity of the existing parties, the entrenched loyalty towards existing parties and the well established voting patterns in this country. These two factors militate against the undesirable proliferation of political parties in Canada, and the requirement for the deposit of $200 in no way furthers that desirable objective.
As matters now stand, the deposit of $200 is large enough to deter those in straitened financial circumstances but too small to deter those who are determined to disturb the electoral process. It acts against the poor and does not deter anyone of normal financial means from deliberately meddling in the political process and perverting its purposes. We have seen that happening. The $200 deposit requirement will become a total farce if, as I suspect, at some future date this Parliament considers legislation which will provide financial aid from the public purse to bona fide political parties. So, I would simply recommend the elimination of the $200 deposit. It is useless in that it does not achieve its purpose, and it will eventually be rendered farcical when political parties are supported by the public purse.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant

I listened with interest to the arguments of the hon. member. I cannot support them. I believe there is a tendency for frivolous candidates to offer themselves in an election. I respect the desire to give the maximum opportunity to those who genuinely

represent a serious point of view to participate in the democratic process. The simple truth is that in municipal elections, where there is no deposit required, it is almost routine procedure for candidates who are not serious to offer themselves for office, sometimes even those who are a little mentally disturbed. There has to be some kind of restriction on this type of candidacy.
There is another situation which gives me concern. I feel that the deposit and the return of the deposit should be tied in with meeting the requirements of the Act, including a statement of election expenses. I may possibly offer an amendment in that respect at a later stage. First, I think we have to defeat any proposal to eliminate the deposit. In my opinion it would be a retrograde step. It is a fairly nominal sum. It has not been changed for a substantial period of time. I do not think it has discouraged people with a genuine party or other interest from presenting themselves as a choice to the electorate. For these reasons, I oppose the argument of the hon. member.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wish to add a few comments to the point of view which has been expressed. My information is that the figure of $200 has been in the Canada Elections Act since the year 1882, when it was raised from $50. I do not quite agree with the hon. member in his rationale. I agree with the hon. member for Ottawa West who has pointed out it is not so much in relation to the party system as in relation to frivolous candidacies, such as a group calling themselves the Rhinoceros party or individuals who are self-advertisers.
It might well be that the figure of $200 is not a sufficient deterrent or threshold. The provisions in Manitoba and Quebec are the same as at the federal level. In Ontario there is no deposit required, but on the other hand the signatures of 100 electors are required. In the province of British Columbia, the signatures of 50 electors are required. I think most members will agree the purpose is a deterrent against frivolous candidacies. I disagree with the hon. member that it will become meaningless when in time we deal with the question of election expenses.
I think my memory is correct when I say that one of the comments of the Barbeau Committee was the possibility of the deposit being raised and part of it being returned to the candidate after he has filed the election return required of him under the election expense regime. As I already said, the com-
June 23. 1970

Canada Elections Act
mittee will be considering that in due course. It seems that the basic reasons for including it in the first place continue. Indeed, the committee may not only decide to leave it at the present level, but to raise it or change the circumstances under which it is required.

The President of the Privy Council has somewhat accurately described the situation in British Columbia with respect to provincial election laws. It is true that no deposit is required. The requirement of 50 signatures applies if there are 10,000 or more registered voters in a constituency. If there are less than 10,000 registered voters, 25 signatures are required for nomination. The President of the Privy Council did not mention that aspect.
I have had personal experience and Involvement in campaigns in the province of British Columbia dating back to 1952. This Involved quite a number of provincial elections. Although there may have been one or two instances, I cannot recall so-called frivolous candidates entering the race in British Columbia in any elections or by-elections that have been held since 1952. It may well be that someone could say that all of the candidates of all parties are frivolous candidates. However, that is an argumentative point. It has equal validity to anyone who puts forward that argument. My basic point is that I cannot recall any frivolous candidates running in these elections. All of the candidates with whom I have had experience ran under the label of a political party, and we have quite a number of them in British Columbia, or as independent serious-minded candidates with a large background and support.
The experience we have had in British 'Columbia is that the lack of a deposit requirement has not attracted the frivolous kind of candidate who enters the race to gain publicity or to embark on a bit of hobbycraft or a game of that sort. I do not know what the experience has been in the province of Ontario. Some members from Ontario may wish to comment on that. The argument that a deposit of any amount deters the entry of so-called frivolous candidates has a false base. The experience in British Columbia proves that it is false. There is no such monetary deterrent to candidates running in an election. As a consequence since 1952, and I am sure many years prior to that, the so-called frivolous candidates have not entered provincial elections.

I wish to take issue with the hon. member for Skeena on this point. It is rather difficult to discuss frivolous candidates without using their names. This I do not choose to do. From my experience in British Columbia, I can recall at least one totally frivolous candidate who ran in a provincial election. He invented a party for the purpose of entering a party name. That particular case involved a by-election. This man did no campaigning and had very little interest in the election, yet it cost the public money. Similarly, moving from the provincial to the civic field, for many years in Vancouver, which has a greater population than one or two provinces, candidates have run for the office of mayor whom I would consider frivolous. I recall one candidate who wanted to tear up the main street and substitute a canal. While I do not recall any frivolous candidates running under the standard party labels, I can recall the occasional oddball in other elections.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I wish to add to the list of frivolous candidates the one in England who recently changed his name in order to run with the same name as Mr. Heath. I wish to point out how far he got.

The same thing has happened in parts of Canada; candidates with similar names were brought in simply to confuse the electorate. But as the President of the Privy Council pointed out earlier there has in fact been a reduction in the real value of this $200 deposit because of the decline in the purchasing power of the dollar, if for no other reason. If the 25 signatures to the petition put up $8 apiece they would finance the entry of their candidate in the election race, and it seems to me this is a minimum sign of confidence in the ability of a man or a woman to be a candidate.

Perhaps I might comment briefly on what hon. members have said with regard to this proposal. It seems to me that most of them have demonstrated that the $200 deposit does not, in fact, work as a deterrent to frivolous candidates. Otherwise, all the frivolous candidates mentioned would not have been involved. Any person who is determined to be a frivolous candidate can raise the sum. What I am saying is that serious candidates are being penalized financially for contesting an election. For example, each of the candidates opposing me in my

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes. I am sorry. I thought the hon. member said "eight or nine". Apparently he said "(h) and (i)". It is quite in order.

These two paragraphs have the effect of permitting a party label to be put on the ballot, or they permit a candidate to be described as an independent. I think all of us would agree that where the names of candidates are similar or confusing, some provision should be made for placing the party label on the ballot. Although the provision is permissive in its terms, the result in practice will be

that the party label will go on the ballot in all circumstances. This raises a question as to whether the practice is really desirable.
It is my contention that if the names are not confusing it is undesirable that the party label should appear on the ballot. My reasoning is this: there has been a tendency in recent years for political parties to be merchandised much in the same way as commercial products. However, one great problem in carrying out a successful merchandising effort has been that at the point of sale, namely, the polling booth, the party label has not been in evidence. This means that a candidate during the election has an extremely important function to perform, which is to make known to the electors that he is the candidate for a particular party. If the party label were allowed to appear on the ballot it would mean that the central organization, having the benefit of large election funds and having access to radio and television coverage, would be able to merchandise the entire party; there would be no need to get individual assistance from the candidates in establishing the connection between the large-scale merchandising effort carried on by the central office and the candidate in a particular constituency. In other words, the functions and the responsibility of a candidate would be greatly diminished.
My suggestion is, therefore, that party labels should not appear on the ballots as a general rule. If the vital function of the ordinary candidate in an election campaign were diminished it would mean that the importance of individual Members of Parliament would likewise be reduced; the degree of independence they possess would be lessened.
If there is any support for my proposal, I would move that paragraphs (h) and (i) of subclause (2) be deleted and replaced by a provision which would permit party labels to be used when there was some good reason for doing so, for example, if names of candidates were similar or confusing. To avoid wasting the time of the committee I shall not move an amendment unless I see there is some support for my proposal.
