The general reasoning behind this amendment, which would have greater application in a metropolitan or urban area than in a rural area, is that it is not uncommon in these areas for people to have to drive for an hour, an hour and a half or in some cases two hours from their residence to place of work. Admittedly, there is a clause further on in the bill which provides that every person shall be entitled to a three-hour period away from his employment without loss of pay, to take account of this sort of thing; but nevertheless, in urban areas people have to contend with traffic conditions, pressures of life, and so on, and this does lead to delay.
In the community of Prince Rupert there are a number of urban polling divisions, and when the polls have closed at seven o'clock I have known of instances where in this city of something like 15,000 people voters have reached the polls too late to vote even though they have made every effort to get there before time. This amendment is an attempt to broaden the opportunity for electors to get to the polling station by providing them with a little extra time in the evening. If I am not mistaken, prior to the last amendment to the Elections Act in 1960 the hours were set at from eight to eight. I could be wrong about that. Perhaps I am thinking of provincial jurisdictions which provide for a 12-hour voting period, which does give a little extra time to those who may be inconvenienced by pressures of traffic and distance away from home to cast their ballot. Industrial workers often prefer to go home, have their dinner and change their clothes before going to the polls. This amendment would give them additional opportunity to exercise their democratic right at their own convenience.
Canada Elections Act [Translation]

Mr. Chairman, I have nothing against the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) designed to extend the closing time of polling stations by one hour.
However, it seems to me that they should be opened one hour later in the morning. I wonder if the opening of the polls at nine o'clock instead of eight could not be considered. In fact, on four election days, I realized that, at least in my riding, the number of voters who show up at the polls at the beginning of the day is very small indeed. Election workers must be at the polls very early in the morning and have to wait two or three hours before voters start coming.
I would therefore support the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena proposing that polls remain open until 8 o'clock at night, and that, at the same time, an opening time of 9 o'clock in the morning instead of 8 be considered.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, usually, elections are held in summer when daylight saving time is in force. If the polls open at nine o'clock instead of eight; this would in fact mean at 10 a.m.
But, many people like to vote in the morning, on their way to work, and I suggest that, if the polls open at 10 o'clock, this would be a bit late. That would also be the case if they closed at 9 o'clock instead of 8 o'clock. The results of the voting, which everyone is eager to know, would also be delayed one hour.

Mr. Chairman, I have no objection at all to this amendment. When we last made a major amendment in 1960, if I recall aright, we added one hour; it used to be six o'clock. I have had no testimony from anybody involved in the electoral process that this hour has been insufficient. I agree with what the Parliamentary Secretary said about the effect of daylight saving time.
If there is in the mind of the hon. member a real need for this extra hour, I certainly would not object to the amendment, though it would make for longer hours for poll workers and would also delay the national returns. But unless there is a fairly clearly demonstrated necessity for the amendment, I see no point in it. We must always remember that we have the protection afforded by the three-hour period away from duty.
I am not quite happy with the suggestion of my hon. friend to my far left in regard to

June 23, 1970
Canada Elections Act
cutting off the morning hours. A lot of people vote en route to work, especially in the heart of the city, so perhaps it is not wise to leave opening time until late in the morning. Although I have no strong views either way, I am not sure that the amendment is necessary.

Neither am I, Mr. Chairman, except that I would suggest that if you add an extra hour either in the morning or in the afternoon, you will have to revise your cost and fees legislation to meet the minimum wage scale and pay them $22.28 a day.

Mr. Chairman, I have one argument to add to those made by my colleague from Skeena. We must remember that this act applies to by-elections as well as to general elections. I recently experienced a byelection. Despite the provision in the Elections Act that an employee must be granted at least three hours in which to cast his vote, in a by-election it is very difficult for some employees to get their employer to grant them that right. My experience was that a great many people missed voting because they were unable to get to the polling station from their place of employment by 7 p.m.. I think the extra hour would be worth while, especially in a by-election where there is no great insistence that the three-hour period be honoured.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Leader of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have not taken part in this debate but I rise to ask the minister whether he would consider the suggestion that has been made. He has not commented on it, but it is obvious he does not agree with it. When I was first elected to Parliament in 1962 I had been active, as hon. members know, in the practice of law on behalf of labour. On numerous occasions during elections that took place between 1950 and 1962 I was asked by union clients to telephone employers to tell them they must let their people go to the polls in time, or else.
The fact is that despite the provision in the act there are many employers in the country who simply do not observe it. I am not condemning them. There are many small employers with only a few employees who cannot afford to pay for three hours taken out of a week's work. Unless the employees or their union make a fuss, they do not get time to vote. I could go back to my files and cite many examples where precisely this sort of thing has occurred.
Nowadays work often finishes at five o'clock or shortly thereafter. Even in industrial plants some shifts finish earlier than that.
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
If there were an extra hour available until eight o'clock, there is no doubt that everybody would be able to attend the polling station. But in many cases the seven o'clock .deadline is simply too soon. I do not think anybody would suffer from the extra hour being allowed. The hon. member to my right said it would delay the national returns, and this might have been true before instant communication, before results appeared almost instantaneously across the country, subject to the time zones that have to be observed. I do not think that now presents any difficulty at all. As a result of radio and television, results are flashed across the country very quickly. They may be delayed an hour, of course, but they will not be delayed to the point where that evening the effective results would not be known to every Canadian.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
The effective result as to the trend, which party is leading and how the parties rank is now known at eight o'clock if you are on standard time, one hour after the polls close, and they would be known at nine o'clock, one hour after the polls closed at eight. That is certainly not any loss to the country or to the election process, whereas to disenfranchise thousands of Canadians because of an early closing of the polls is, I suggest, a very serious loss to the country and to the electoral process. I would therefore urge hon. members, and particularly the minister, to accept the very reasonable suggestion that we extend it one hour in the evening to enable thousands more people to exercise their democratic right. I repeat, that with instant communication no one and nothing would suffer because of that extension.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I take no strong stand on this matter one way or the other, but I do not agree with the hon. gentleman. From my experience, at the times that he and I have been running in general elections in our cities I have not found there to be any difficulty at all with the existing hours in the Elections Act. I regard this as a case not proven. It seems to me that with our time span there is time enough for virtually everyone to vote. The hon. member says no one would suffer. I suppose one could say the polls staffs would suffer by having to work an extra hour at the polls.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Leader of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, would the minister excuse me for asking a loaded question? Is the minister aware of the fact that before
June 23, 1970

distribution I had a section in my riding, Forest Hill Village, which did not suffer from the hours of polling. I suppose part of Rose-dale may be in the same situation.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Let me point out to the hon. gentleman, if he thinks there is some virtue in representing a low-income area and that it is something to boast about, that my area is undoubtedly a lower income area than his. I am thinking in terms of Regent Park and other parts of the city. I do not know what his observation is in that regard.
I would only say that it does seem to me there has been no evidence of disenfranchisement. It is true that 76 per cent of the electors on the electoral lists voted in the last election. I think that percentage is right. This means that 24 per cent did not vote. I have seen no evidence, and we have had no evidence put before us this evening, that this occurred because of the hours of polling. I remain unconvinced, like the hon. member for Hillsborough, about the necessity for this amendment. I suppose on this particular point each member should vote as his experience indicates. Mine does not indicate the necessity for it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to present a little bit of evidence I have gathered over the years. There are a great many instances where the woman of the house waits until the man gets home from work and they usually get their supper over, get cleaned up and go to the polls together. This is particularly true in a riding like mine, where a great many families have only one car or perhaps do not have a car at all. The woman waits for her husband to get home and they then go to the polls together. I know this is so because we have been troubled at a great many polls by congestion at closing time, particularly in earlier times when the closing hour was earlier. I feel it would be a good idea to add this extra hour to facilitate families-they are very numerous-where the husband and wife make a habit of going to the polls together in the evening.

Mr. Chairman, I hope to make what I feel is another valid point. I am glad to note that the President of the Privy Council is not yet convinced one way or the other, or does not feel very strongly about this matter. I repeat what I know is a principle that every member in this chamber has in mind: our electoral laws must maximize the 22478-49
Canada Elections Act
opportunity for the greatest number of Canadians to exercise their franchise.
Since we were not able to come up with an acceptable absentee balloting system-and I suppose this is the main point-it seems to me we should do everything possible to increase the opportunity to cast a ballot. A few amendments have already been accepted and many ideas have been put forward. I believe this is another way, although it might be considered a small point, in which the opportunity to cast a ballot would be enlarged. Surely that is a principle with which no one in this chamber would disagree.
I support the points made earlier by some of my colleagues in relation to the extra hour in the evening, particularly because of the kind of society we now have. We live in urban and suburban areas. People start doing things when they get home from their work, and presumably on election day one of the things they will do is vote. It is more likely that they will vote during that hour because it is more convenient for them. I suggest again that our electoral laws should make it as convenient as possible for voters to cast their ballots. If I were to support any change, I would prefer to see the polls open an hour later in the morning. Our amendment still refers to eight o'clock in the morning, the same as the hour proposed in the bill, but we ask for an additional hour in the evening. A number of reasons have been put forward which I hope will convince those members who are willing to be convinced that this is a worth-while change.

Mr. Chairman, having considered this clause I feel it is very reasonable as it stands. I agree with the Government House Leader that 11 hours is long enough. Moreover, I would remind the committee that if polling day is lengthened the staff will have to be paid that much more. This will increase election expenses borne by the taxpayer. Under the modern conditions of 1970, anyone who cannot get to the polls to vote after finishing work at five o'clock must work a long way from the poll. I do not believe that many people in this day and age work so far away from the poll they cannot get there by seven o'clock. For that reason I support the clause as it is.

Mr. Chairman, the matter may mean additional expenses, but it is the taxpayer we are concerned about and providing him with a fair opportunity to cast a ballot. The President of the Privy Council

June 23, 1970
Canada Elections Act
has said that as far as he and the government are concerned they have no strong views one way or the other, and that we should approach this question on the basis of our individual experience. I think we must consider that suggestion together with an understanding of what is individual experience. Let me refer to the city of Prince Rupert, which has a group of urban polling divisions. In my experience, people there have missed getting to the poll because of the closing time and the distance they have had to travel.
Let me expand upon that by relating the situation to some rural polling stations on the coast of British Columbia. In some areas of Vancouver Island, loggers have travelling time, that is, the time it takes to get from home to work out in the bush, and vice versa. This time in certain areas ranges up to 2J or 21 hours. Some people have to leave home at 5.30 or a quarter to six to catch the "crummy" at the marshalling point and get to work out in the bush by eight o'clock.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
If you reverse this situation, assuming that the polls close at seven o'clock, with standard time in existence at the time of the election the individual receives three hours off from employment, which means he would have to leave his job out in the bush at four o'clock. We might couple that with up to 2J- hours spent in travelling from out in the bush to his home where the polling division should be. There is a half-hour leeway, which is not very much when you take into account the difficulties which might arise.
I have ridden on these "crummies" in logging camps. Sometimes they have flat tires, and during the early winter and late winter there is a very inclement weather, snow or wetness, which causes difficulty in travelling. Travelling under such conditions may take two hours or more, and in such a case the individual would miss the opportunity to vote simply because he worked at a spot which was far away from his place of residence. In many cases it is impossible for him to make the journey in time, even taking into account the three hours he is permitted to be away from his employment.
This is recognized under the elections act of British Columbia. In British Columbia provincial elections the employee is entitled to four hours free time from his employment. That takes into account the additional factor of having to travel long distances in certain areas. In rural areas in southern Ontario and
[Mr. Howard (Skeena) .J
in urban metropolitan centres, sometimes a person has to travel a long distance, but the same problems are not involved. I earnestly plead that this factor be given consideration. I do not think our consideration should be based entirely on the concept of its costing so much money, because our democratic process does cost money. But I believe we have a commitment in terms of spending that money in order to provide the fullest opportunity to voters to cast their ballots.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was not thinking of the money involved but, rather, the extra hour the polls people would have to work. However, the hon. member has talked me into it. Let us see if he has persuaded anybody else.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Vice-Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the proposal of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) is worthless. In fact, the act stipulates that the employer must give his employees three hours to vote. If an employee leaves at 4 o'clock and cannot get to the poll by 7 o'clock it is because he is too far away. The legislation provides that these people may vote at an advance poll a week before the election.
I wonder how the hon. member for Skeena can imagine that someone who is unable to get to a polling station before 7 o'clock, because he is absent that day, cannot report at an advance poll a week before the election in order to exercise his franchise.
I think that it will not change anything to the act, and the arguments that he puts forward in order to justify adding an additional hour to polling time may apply in all circumstances. But if somebody is able to prove that he is absent from his electoral district on polling day, he may be allowed to cast his ballot a week before at an advance poll.
Therefore, I do not believe that the argument of the hon. member for Skeena is of any value.

Mr. Chairman, I feel obliged to come back to the question that I raised earlier.
As I consider the opening and closing hours of the polling stations, I note that the election workers have to report to the polling station, at least half an hour before opening time. And if we reckon as an average another half an hour to go to the polling stations which, in summer, open at nine o'clock in the morning,
June 23, 1970

these people will have to leave their house at eight o'clock in order to be there in time.
And after the closing of the poll, at eight o'clock, daylight saving time, it takes about an hour to count the ballots and another half hour to go back home. That means that our election workers have to put in a 14 hour-day because, at the dinner hour, there is no closing of the polls.
It is a work day far too long, since the number of electors registered at each polling station generally does not exceed 300. Therefore, if we are unable in 10 or 11 hours to get these people to vote, something is wrong somewhere. As a matter of fact, that may indicate that the polling stations are badly located and that we should endeavour to put them in the centre of the electoral district.
If the election takes place in summer, the polling stations will open at nine o'clock. I believe in winter, fall or spring they should also open not earlier than 9 a.m.
Turning to the argument just put forward by the hon. member for Skeena to the effect that the voter can leave his job at 4 to go to the polling station, I believe that if polling hours are extended by one hour he will not leave at 4, but at 5, since his employer will not have to give him an hour off. He will still have only three horns to get to his polling station.
He will be no better off. Unless it is agreed to start the polling day an hour later in the morning, I must vote against the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena.

Mr. Chairman, on page 96, subclause (6) of clause 33 reads as follows:
A returning officer may, where he deems it advisable, establish a central polling place where the polling stations of all or any of the polling divisions
Canada Elections Act
of any locality may be centralized, except that no central polling place so established shall comprise more than ten polling divisions unless it is the usual practice in a locality to establish a central polling place for civic, municipal or provincial elections and the Chief Electoral Officer has given his prior permission for the establishment of a central polling place comprising more than ten polling divisions.
Mr. Chairman, this subclause is disputable. In my constituency, I found that for two different elections at least, in a particular town, eight polling stations were centralized in the same hall. But nobody had thought of providing an easy access to that hall. It had only one door and an election worker who was posted at the door allowed the electors to enter the room only one by one. So five or six days would have been necessary to allow all electors to cast their ballots into the ballot boxes!
On each occasion, I had to discuss and argue to be authorized to open the doors and let the electors in that large hall so that they might reach the polls.
Corrective measures should be taken in this connection. I wonder whether it would not be better to make the act state that such central polling places be set up in such a way that electors may be directed by persons employed by the returning officer to the polls where they must vote, so as not to delay unduly the other voters.
To that effect, it is my intention, if this is suitable, Mr. Chairman, to move the following amendment:
That Bill C-215, an Act respecting the franchise of electors and the election of members to the House of Commons, be amended by deleting the period at the end of subclause 6 of clause 33, line 18, on page 96 thereof, and adding thereto the following:

Mr. Chairman, I should like to move an amendment to subclause (1) of clause 39. Seconded by the member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin) I move:
That subclause (1) of clause 39 be amended by adding after the words "to be required of him" the following:
"if he is not carrying his identification card bearing his photo and duly approved by the governor in council".
I should like to make a few remarks in this connection.
According to the present act, the persons assigned to drawing up voters lists go to every home where they ask the name of the citizens, male and female, who live there and have the right to vote. Voters lists are made up in duplicate and each voter get a copy of the list of his area.
In some rural areas, the citizens exercise their franchise in a proportion of 80 per cent. There is no problem. But, in large cities, where people lose interest in politics, the proportion may be of 20 to 30 per cent. However, it happens that citizens who are not interested in politics are interested in money and they manage to earn a few dollars by selling their copy of the enumerator's notice to elector. The cost of those copies which allows the elector to vote is usually around $5. Families of five individuals with the right to vote are very happy with the present system and they feel they are doing good business since, without even having to go out, they can make $25 on election day.
Under these circumstances, it is the party with the best election funds which will be able to buy the greatest number of copies and have its candidate elected.
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) .1
If the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) so desires, I could bring him an election organizer, a man responsible for a "telegraph office," who was in charge of outfitting about a hundred people who, on a certain election day, cast about ten ballots each. I am sure that an identity card is not as easy to trade as the registration copy for which there is such a high demand in the present system. It is to complement the bill now before us that I propose this amendment.
Since there is nothing new in this suggestion and since this method is already applied in a number of countries, I do hope, Mr. Chairman, I will have the support of the majority of the members who are still in favour of truly honest elections.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the amendment moved by the hon. member for Porneuf (Mr. Godin) is very timely, because in many countries, everybody has an identification card bearing his photo and must carry it with him, otherwise he could be penalized.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one of the difficulties about the proxy voting system is the increased risk of loss of control, in the sense that there may be loss of assurance of the relative fidelity of the voting system. There are two principles involved here. The first is the principle which motivated the hon. member to give to the maximum number of people the opportunity of voting in an election. There is, on the other hand, the generally desirable attitude that controls over the voting system should be relatively efficacious and that so far as possible we should prevent fraud, personation, and so on.
The problem with personation under our present system exists normally where individual A, knowing that individual B is an elector on the list of a poll and has not yet gone to the poll, goes to the polling station and represents himself to be B and votes in his stead. That is a simple case of personation. The protection against this-I acknowledge it is not very effective protection in the case of an urban poll-is the possibility that he will be recognized by someone at the poll as not being the individual he holds himself out to be. There have been a number of such cases in recent years.
The problem of proxy voting is that there is the risk of personation at one stage further; that is to say, an individual may go to a poll and represent as to a document, on which he or someone else may have forged the signature of an elector, that that is the signature of the absent person. It is difficult at the best of times to know the identity of an elector at an urban poll or, for that matter, at a rural poll and very few people-I think hon. members will recognize this from their own experience-will know the exact signature of an elector. So there is a greater risk of personation in such circumstances. For that reason I understand the committee confined itself to a relatively limited number of situations where it would be physically impossible for individuals to attend at the poll and they would have to appoint an agent for this purpose.
The case which had the greatest appeal for me and for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, because of a common friend, was that of persons who because of illness or physical incapacity are incapable of leaving their residence and going to the poll. There you would be least likely to have a case of personation.
June 23, 1970

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: That is the most important case, moreover.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that is the most important case. The other two cases are occupational ones and an argument could be raised-indeed, I raised it myself on second reading-as to whether a more general wording might be applied such as, "All persons who, by the nature of their occupation, will not be able to be present either at the advance poll or at the poll on election day." It has been pointed out to me, however, that owing to the problem I have just mentioned, the risk of personation, the wording should be fairly restrictive. To the extent that we extend this provision to one occupational group we shall invite arguments as to why it should not be extended to other groups, thereby raising the risk of personation and of damage being done.
The occupations which have been cited here are fishermen, mariners and prospectors. In the case of both fishermen and mariners, you have occupations where voters are very commonly on the waters and absent from the community for a period which could cover both the advanced poll and polling day. In the same way, prospectors carry on their activities far removed from the normal places of residence in this country; that is to say, in remote areas where they do not have access to a poll.
I would express at this point my great reluctance to extending the group any further in this regard, although I will be glad to hear the views of hon. members on this point, particularly on the question whether by extending the vote to one industry we should extend it to others and thereby risk the integrity of the system.

Mr. Chairman, this is one part of the bill, and indeed one part of the committee report, which has caused me the most concern. The introduction of proxy voting is, in the minds of many members, a compromise. Certainly so far as I am concerned, it is second best. I think we will really cover people who are not able physically to be at the place of voting only when we adopt a system of absentee voting whereby these people can get their ballot to the poll without being there themselves.
I think we must bear in mind that a proxy vote is a diluted vote. It represents some diminution of the will of the person to whom the vote is extended because he cannot control, so long as the poll remains secret, what
Canada Elections Act
happens. That is why I still believe we shall achieve only second best so long as in our country we avoid what has been done in other countries, namely, the establishment of a permanent voters' list as a result of which we can establish a system of absentee voting. Then we shall not have an abridged type of franchise by means of the proxy vote. When you start enumerating lists it is quite difficult to be all-encompassing and cover every one.
I remember one election in which a very large and prominent church happened to hold its national assembly. The assembly had begun before the advanced poll began, and those worthy and religious men, except the ones that happened to be resident at the site of the convention, were not able to vote. In our mobile society this sort of thing happens constantly and is not confined to mariners, fishermen and others like them. The group I am concerned about are the patients in nonchronic hospitals-I think this provision would be very useful to them-and the people who are at home and incapable of going to the poll.
I do not like the suggestion that students should vote in this way. I cannot see a student having his "old man" or his mother casting his vote back home for him. I think that is degrading of his rights as a voting citizen. I think the former system was far better even though in 1965, because of unfortunate timing, the country lost the votes of some of these people. It is second-hand voting and, as someone else has suggested, it is not a good thing. I am more kindly disposed to the system being extended to patients in nonchronic hospitals, nursing homes and institutions of that kind. However, I see great danger in all this and we delude ourselves if we think we are extending the full franchise. We are extending something less than the full franchise. I can only accept it as second best, and not a close second at that.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)

On second reading of this bill, Mr. Chairman, I said that I intended to introduce an amendment to extend proxy voting to loggers. I have a particular concern in this matter, as do other members from British Columbia and other parts of Canada. Loggers are one group particularly discriminated against by the lack of the absentee ballot. The amendment now before us is similar to the amendment I intended to introduce with regard to loggers. I have since had time to study the lengthy deliberations of the com-

June 23. 1970
Canada Elections Act
mittee on this matter. I have had conversation with officers of the Crown regarding this matter. Difficulties present themselves in extending proxy voting to one class of citizens such as loggers, and not to others, or to a broad class of citizens. Simply to introduce the proxy vote to anyone who in the course of his occupation is likely to be away from his place of residence appears to introduce so many possibilities of misuse, fraud and impersonation that I have reluctantly come to the conclusion that the extension of proxy voting beyond the very narrow categories listed here is not a very workable solution.
I have also come to this conclusion with regard to the cl mses which were stood earlier today in the committee's deliberations-clause 17 of the bill, as well as clauses 9 and 10, and specifically clauses 12 and 13. I believe worthwhile amendments could be introduced here and I intend to introduce them at the appropriate time. While they will not provide the vote to all Canadians who by reason of their occupation have to be absent from their place of registration on voting day or on advance polling day, I think the franchise could be extended very considerably by amendments to these clauses. In fact, I am particularly attracted to this way of doing it because the form of the amendments I intend to introduce will not specify loggers, construction workers or any other class of worker. However, it will have general application to anyone who by reason of his occupation must be absent from the polling division in which they are registered on voting day or on advance polling day.
With some regret I have been driven back from the position I took when I first recommended absentee balloting and absentee balloting under a permanent voters' list, which as was pointed out by the hon. member for Hillsborough is the most desirable way of meeting this situation. In its wisdom, the committee found this not to be feasible. I agree with the hon. member for Hillsborough that proxy voting is a compromise. It is not as good as we might hope for, but it is better than nothing. It has limited application.
I hope the committee will agree that I can put forward an amendment to clause 17 concerning a permanent voters' list. The system could be improved considerably to enable a great many more Canadians whose occupations force them to be absent from their polling divisions on voting day or on advance polling day, to cast their vote.

Mr. Chairman, I have mixed feelings about this amendment. My basic inclination is to support it. I am aware of the difficulties of too rapidly broadening the base of voting by proxy. While we are dealing generally with these categories I wish to qualify my opposition to the amendment now before us. The committee might think of it in the context that there is one exception which had a reasonable amount of consideration in the committee. I refer to the exception of elderly or other people who for one reason or another are confined to nursing homes.
The bill requires that a medical certificate be obtained in the case of illness or incapacitation. It is very difficult to get a doctor to issue a medical certificate for an elderly person who may be in a nursing home, hospital or rest home and who is neither ill nor incapacitated but because of age and infirmity is not able to go to a poll to vote. I say there are exceptions. I do not think the President of the Privy Council should be so firm and rigid in his opposition to broadening the system where there are justifiable grounds.
When the amendment now before us is dealt with, I intend to move an amendment to the effect that after the words "illness or physical incapacity" something along the following lines be added, "a patient in a hospital recognized by one or more of the several provinces and/or a patient in a nursing home recognized in one or more of the several provinces". That will take care of people in that specific category. I think the category in the context of the present amendment is a little too broad and could lend itself to abuse. I suggest by way of contrast, that people in nursing homes and similar institutions are not in the same capacity. Many members in this chamber may have parents who are in nursing homes or other institutions of this type. We had a lengthy discussion on this clause when it was before the committee. The committee agreed to at least one useful amendment. With regard to the proposal originally considered by the committee, it was established that the committee was prepared in principle to look at occupational groups, and where there was a clearly identifiable group, the committee was prepared to include these people in their new adventure in voting. I will speak to this matter later.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I suggest this is one category that is clearly identifiable and for which there can be no broadening, expansion or contraction at the
June 23, 1970

time of the prosecution of a general election or by-election. The present amendment does not meet this requirement. It is too broad. It is conceivable that there will be people who travel, such as truck drivers, airline pilots and those in the transportation industry, who by virtue of their day-to-day work will not be able to exercise their franchise on voting day or on advance polling day. In the case of identifiable groups we should ensure, while we have the opportunity to do so, that they are not excluded. But when they are not controllable units, when they cannot be defined, we must be extremely careful not to open the door to possible abuse.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want clause 46 to pass without expressing my pleasure on finding university students included in those covered by the proxy voting procedure. Hon. members may recall that in September, 1965, thousands of students in universities across Canada were disenfranchised because they were caught between the time of the issuing of the writ and the time of taking up residence. For five years I set down on the Order Paper public bills offering a method of correcting this situation.
I presume we are all glad to see it corrected now, as far as this can be done through the proxy vote procedure. I express my thanks to the members of the Standing Committee and especially to the chairman, my hon. friend from Montmorency, for permitting me to appear before the committee and appeal on behalf of students that the act should be changed so as to enable them to vote should an election again be called in the circumstances of 1965.

Mr. Chairman, when 1 was much younger and much less flabby I used to be a logger. As a result of that experience I began working toward a system of absentee balloting applicable not only to loggers but to others who followed occupations which kept them away from their ordinary residences or meant their moving from one residence to another. The hon. member for Coast Chilcotin is familiar with this situation.
The hon. member for Hillsborough and I were the two members of the Standing Committee this year who were also members of the same Standing Committee in 1960 when the last major revision of the Elections Act was undertaken. In that year, those of us who advocated an absentee system of balloting were not able to get much support in the 22478-50
Canada Elections Act
committee or, for that matter, any support. As a matter of fact, I had to prevail upon the hon. member for Ottawa West to support me in order to get a motion before the committee for its consideration. I did not realize at that time that a seconder was not needed.
At any rate, after determining that there was no support in the committee for the idea of absentee balloting, for what were obviously valid reasons, I advanced the idea of a proxy system of voting because such a system existed in Ontario for mariners and perhaps for those in other occupations. Again, the idea got nowhere. I was its only supporter. When the committee began to consider this session the question of proxy voting, I wished to extend the principle to include workers in every occupation one could think of, because I was so wedded to the idea of providing a voting opportunity for as many people as possible who normally are disenfranchised by reason of the demands of their occupations.
As I began by saying, I worked in the logging industry on the west coast; I know the difficulties the loggers encounter and realize they are shared by large numbers of miners and construction workers. The Standing Committee spent a long time dealing with the principal point enunciated by the President of the Privy Council, namely, that one must be extremely cautious about extending a facility such as this, bearing in mind the liabilities which might result from such action in terms of personation, duplication of voting and the like. The opinion was expressed that proxy voting should be confined in the main to those who would not normally have an opportunity to get to any polling station.
Earlier, we had prepared amendments covering loggers and construction workers. We reflected on the matter very seriously and in the end decided not to proceed with them because of the inherent difficulties likely to result from their application. I think the present approach is probably a good way of dealing with this question as far as it concerns a large group of workers who, unlike transportation workers, do not have a set destination or a set place of employment. Transportation workers fall into a special category. Normally they work on what is called a run. They set out for the turn-around point, at which they might spend some time, and then they return to their point of origin. So I think we can draw a distinction between transport workers and larger groups of workers, which it is virtually impossible to identify except in the most general terms, engaged in work of a

June 23. 1970
Canada Elections Act
transient nature, or people who work in areas where they are located only temporarily.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I urge general support of the concept advanced by my hon. friend from Regina-Lake Centre, recognizing the difficulties encountered by this large group of people who work in areas where they are only temporarily located. I hope, too, that hon. members will endorse the proposal made by the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin when we return to clause 17. If we do this, we shall be moving with all necessary care and attention to preserving the integrity of the balloting system and protecting it against abuses which can and do develop within it. We shall be advancing properly and carefully in the direction we want, namely, that of providing the best opportunity to the greatest number of people to cast their ballots.

Mr. Chairman, my colleague said that I do not agree with him, but this is only partly true. I think if we are to have a proxy voting system it should be extended to as many people as possible. I am sure no one would disagree with the idea of as many people as possible casting their ballots in the way they wish. I am sympathetic to what has been said in favour of proxy votes, but I should like to extend the system. When elections are held during the school year, most students become disqualified from voting because they are away from their normal place of residence. I think we should give consideration more to a system of absentee voting than proxy voting. This would allow the voter to make his own decision.
Sometimes people are prevented from voting simply because they are incapacitated and cannot cast their ballot. There was a poem written by someone in my riding which I should like to read to the committee. Perhaps fortunately, I do not have it with me. It is about a galloping ballot box in a provincial election held in Timiskaming. One of the candidates had a big car and he conveyed the three scrutineers, the deputy returning officer, the clerk and the ballot box to a number of houses in the area to enable people living there to cast their ballots. Many ballots in that election were cast in kitchens, bedrooms and such places which were visited one hour before the polls closed, and this was because a good many people had not been able to vote. Although this was highly illegal, and at the same time somewhat hilarious, none of the candidates in the election-my father was

one-pressed any charges relating to an infraction of the act because all of them believed it had been a good idea to let Mrs. Jones vote, and also Mr. Smith who had been confined to his home with a broken leg. In effect, they moved the polling station to the homes of the voters.
I have suggested on previous occasions that elections should be held every four years at a time when they did not conflict with students' activities. But I would not like to see our enthusiastic young people take advantage of the situation. I know there is some protection in a declaration having to be made on the preceding Friday by a person who wants to vote by proxy, but with the Postmaster General handling the mails it could take two weeks or more before the notification was received, and there would be no safeguard provided. In that event, young people who are now eligible to vote would be able to vote in two places. In view of what happened in the last election, I would not want this to happen. Nevertheless, the possibility is there. You would have mother voting at home and her son voting in Toronto or wherever his college was located. There are a number of ways of meeting this objective which would be less detrimental than the present system. Many countries have adopted the absentee balloting system and I think our Elections Act should make provision for it, in favour of the present scheme.
I also think the principle of proxy voting is wrong. I can see many more abuses than advantages flowing from this situation. This seems to me a poor substitute for a system that would eliminate abuse and still make it possible for eligible voters to cast their own ballots. It has been pointed out that a number of infirm, elderly and incapacitated people will be able to vote by proxy. I think in this regard the elderly people of the nation are being misjudged. I do not think they would tell anybody how they intended to vote. In many cases they would not even tell their own spouse. They take great satisfaction from the secrecy of the ballot.
We saw that in England.

Neither are they interested in how other people voted. In England they had the same difficulty that we had during the last election; many people were not free to tell their spouses how they voted until after election day. The elderly would not ask their spouse to cast a ballot for them with any
June 23, 1970

assurance, and as a result I think this proxy voting system would be used very little.
If this is the only system that is feasible, the amendment moved by my colleague from Regina should be made applicable to those limited categories of people I have suggested, so they can exercise their franchise on election day. I would support the amendment while still being opposed to the principle of a proxy voting system, which I predict will not last more than one election. I would far sooner see absentee balloting, which I think everybody desires.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)

Just a few words on this particular clause, Mr. Chairman, since I feel strongly about some of the points and principles involved. Clause 46 as submitted to the House by the government arises from the report of the committee and enunciates a new principle in connection with proxy voting. The committee, of course, wrestled with some very real problems in endeavouring to enable the greatest possible number of people to exercise their right to the franchise at an election. However, I have very serious doubts about and disagreements with the principle involved in clause 46 and, as a consequence, with the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre.
I feel we must take into account the very real administrative and mechanical problems that will be involved in making this clause work in an acceptable way. All sorts of problems will exist. The hon. member for Timis-kaming has pointed out some of the problems that will arise as a consequence of this clause. Beyond that, there seems to be a more basic principle involved. It seems to me the principle of proxy voting is basically inconsistent with our democratic process, with our democratic operations, with our society and our nation. I feel it is wrong in principle and that it is inconsistent with the principles of democratic government to enable a voter to transfer his right to vote to someone else, however much we may say-and this will be the fact on many occasions-that the voter who receives the proxy will carry out the wishes of the person granting it.
I feel it is a faulty principle which enables voters to transfer what in fact must be regarded as a sacred right if we are to maintain a democratic society and a democratic government in this country. I believe that extending the principle of proxy voting as has been proposed in clause 46, with the still 22478-504
Canada Elections Act
further extension in the amendment before us, will have an eroding effect upon the election process as we know it. I feel that it will also have an eroding effect in terms of public attitude toward our functioning as a democracy.
I concur with the proposition put forward by the hon. member for Timiskaming, that we should be looking at a system of absentee voting. I feel this is the principle we should be working toward. This system in fact could and would go much further than the proposals before us in fulfilling the objectives sought. We have seen absentee voting in operation in various parts of Canada from time to time. In fact, there have been occasions when problems have arisen in this respect. I could quote instances which have occurred in my own province of Saskatchewan when the government, formed by the party of which I am a supporter, instituted a system of absentee voting. It worked very well for several elections. When it came to the close election in 1964, it was found that there were certain weaknesses in the system which had been established. I suggest that those weaknesses could have been corrected by making changes in the mechanics of the system and that in fact in principle the system was very sound.
Thus, I very much regret that the committee did not come forward with a recommendation for a system of absentee voting. Therefore, I place on record my view that we should be working toward a system of absentee voting rather than a system of proxy voting as is proposed in this bill.

Mr. Chairman, a few
moments ago I rose to indicate that I wanted to move a further amendment. Before I do so, I wonder whether the President of the Privy Council would address himself to the suggestion I made, in a manner which will assist those of us who must find some direction not only in the words of the measure but in the spirit and the intent of this clause. He might

June 23. 1970
Canada Elections Act
lend us of his learned and wise mind by giving an interpretation of the clause. Perhaps he would address himself to the interpretation of clause 46 (1) (b) in terms of whether this provision can be construed to include, as I mentioned a little earlier, the many thousands of elderly people in Canada who are at home, in nursing homes or special care institutions and who, while neither physically ill nor incapacitated, are not capable of going out, for example on a rainy day, on a bad day in the winter or on an exceptionally hot day in the spring or the early fall for the purpose of voting.
I do not know why the hon. member for Saint-Denis is laughing. If he does not care about the elderly people in Canada, that is fine; but I ask him not to laugh at me while I am trying to protect them.
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. My friend knows very well that is not the case. I do not like that remark to be on the record, and that is why I am saying this.

Well, do not laugh. I think this is a serious thing. We would be very remiss in our duty if we went to the extent we have in order to bring in this new concept of voting at federal general elections, and failed to include in the act a clear definition of what we mean. We should have an interpretation by someone in a responsible position. We would be very remiss if by failing to do either of those two things we denied to many hundreds of thousands of elderly Canadians the right to vote. I have in mind those who are mentally alert and are deeply interested in the things that are happening in their country. I think all of us, without going too far back in our personal campaigning experiences, could enumerate many instances of people who wanted to exercise their franchise but were not able to do so. I suggest we now have a vehicle by means of which this can be done.
My interpretation of the situation as it now stands-I hope I am wrong-is that a medical certificate is required. My learned friends who are members of the bar know very well that we had an interesting discussion with the chairman of our committee on this subject, and I appreciate his views. He knows very well that we shall not make a valid judgment based on an emotional matter, but that we shall make a valid judgment based on fact.
If a person should not be ill and not physically incapacitated, a doctor or other respon-

sible authority would not sign a medical certificate saying that he was. Indeed, if I were the person for whom such a certificate was being signed, I think I would resent it. On the other hand, it is quite possible that during the winter, or because of other circumstances, it might be extremely difficult for me to get out to vote. Yet we have in this bill a clause that very nearly covers such a situation. It does not, because it only covers people who are factually ill or factually physically incapacitated to the point where they just cannot get out and do what they would wish to do.
Therefore, it is a question, if not of an amendment then certainly of our hearing a few words on the question of interpretation from the minister who is piloting this bill through the House. He should tell us just what is the intent of clause 46(l)(b). This is a fairly narrow but important point because of the number of people involved. I hope the interpretation on this narrow point will be such that the individual concerned will be able to make a value judgment. The responsibility for making a value judgment which is not necessarily based on fact would be removed from the doctor, the hospital superintendent or whoever the person might be.
I do not believe we have the right to require our professional people to make this type of judgment. On the other hand, I believe there is a very clear deficiency in the clause as it now stands. If the President of the Privy Council would address himself to this point, and if his explanation in terms of what is intended is sufficiently clear and satisfactory to me, there will be no need to move an amendment. This might simplify matters.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for what my opinion on this point is worth, I think that here we are speaking of a medical practitioner in the sense of a doctor, head nurse of an institution or some other person who is from time to time medically treating a person in the group in question-in fact, all those persons who would be making decisions in respect of the health, to use the antonym of the word in the clause, or the physical well-being of the person. These people would be required to give a value judgment which I think would hardly be a judgment of fact such as the hon. member referred.
The hon. member suggested that the medical practitioner and the officials should not give a judgment based on anything other
June 23, 1970

than fact. I think the truth of the matter is that virtually every medical judgment is made, not on fact alone but on professional opinion based on knowledge of the facts concerning the particular individual. This ultimately is a question of opinion and judgment.
In respect of the group the hon. member has in mind, and which I certainly had in mind when advocating this change to the Election Act during the course of the current parliamentary session, I am thinking of those who because of advanced years would have the greatest difficulty. In such a case, probably the advice of their practitioner would be that in the interest of their health they should not go outside their residence, or possibly even outside the room in which, regrettably, they happen to be confined. Under such circumstances I do not have any doubt that this provision would be very broadly construed. A medical practitioner should not have difficulty in signing the kind of certificate which would be required in respect of his patient, in order to give that person an opportunity to vote by proxy.

Mr. Chairman, I think I could find this interpretation quite acceptable. I think it clarifies what is intended in this narrow provision. I think the point the President of the Privy Council is attempting to make is clear, and that returning officers seeking a clear understanding of what is intended by this clause would find the necessary counsel in simply reading the words of the President of the Privy Council. I will accept that as an interpretation.
Subclause 1 agreed to.
Subclauses 2 to 13 inclusive agreed to.

The same principle would apply to subclause 17 and would cover any person who changes his ordinary residence, following the enumeration date, to another polling division in the same electoral district. This would have the effect of removing the rather narrow category referred to in subclause 9 and would broaden it to include anybody who during the time period in question had moved, therefore making it possible for such persons to be put on the voters' list of the district to which they had moved. It arises out of my earlier statement that I had hoped to extend to loggers the clause on proxy voting and for reasons which I need not repeat to the committee this has not proven feasible. As a matter of fact, like many other hon. members I am disturbed that one particular group such as loggers should be chosen in this connection. I have chosen them because they are numerous in my riding. Because of the nature of their occupation, they are often not in the place of their ordinary residence on polling day, or on advance polling day. There are many other people in the same category. Subclause 12 (b) could improve the situation for these workers.
For the benefit of those who are not familiar with west coast logging, I might explain to members of the committee-although I am sure this situation is repeated in respect of different occupations in many other parts of Canada-that it is very difficult for a person employed in the logging industry to be certain where he will be on a date some weeks or months in advance. A great many loggers have their ordinary places of residence in large towns, in the city of Vancouver or elsewhere. Their ordinary place of work is likely to be in extremely isolated areas, isolated by everything except air or sea transport, say, at the head of B.C. coastal inlets. The times of work are irregular. Naturally, they are under a union contract, yet there are many camps where even under the union contract a logger may work three weeks with one week off, which he spends at home. There is the further difficulty in that elections are usually held in the spring, summer or early autumn and during the summer months in British Columbia no one can foresee when a dry season will result in a complete shutdown of the woods industry. I am afraid this is an alteration of the act in the wrong direction. I think this is unreasonable and unnecessary, even to prevent fraud. Of course, fraud is possible in respect of everything we are passing in this committee tonight. In proxy voting there is a danger of impersonation, and in the temporary residence qualification there is the risk of fraud and impersonation. I suggest that it is the duty of the committee to make a good and sound compromise between the dangers of fraud and impersonation and the necessity of extending the franchise, most particularly to people whose livelihood requires their absence from polling divisions. Like a great many members in this House, I am convinced that the only truly satisfactory system, and one which we must eventually adopt, is that of a permanent voters' list and a system of absentee balloting. Mr. Chairman, while the amendment appears lengthy, its substance may be summed up shortly. With my amendment is a subsequent amendment affecting two of the forms in schedule 1. They are attached to the amendment and are being distributed for the sake of clarification. What you have in your hand, sir, is a proposal two pages in length. It is headed "New section 47A." There are also two other forms.
Very simply, the amendment is this: For many years there has been a provision in the act that a qualified elector in a rural polling division whose name is not upon the voters' list for the appropriate polling division may still cast his ballot after taking an oath as to who he is. In it he must undertake other obligations and give information. Also, some-

one who is a registered voter on the voters' list must appear with him, vouch for him and take an oath saying that he knows the person who seeks to vote even though his name is not on the voters' list. This is a fairly common practice in rural polling divisions and it is of advantage to those who for one reason or another are not able to have their names appear on the voters' list or at the court of revision for the rural polling division.
Some people wonder why the same provision is not available in an urban polling division and this has been a cause of concern. This is especially so in areas which at one time were classified as rural polling divisions and because of the growth and development of the area have been reclassified as urban polling divisions. People wonder why in the one case they can follow one procedure and [DOT]take an oath, and then simply because the community or polling division has been reclassified or called by a different name they cannot follow that procedure. I know that many members have been interested in developing a mechanism under which the people of urban polling divisions can take advantage of such a procedure.
Perhaps the suggestion I am making is not thoroughly acceptable. Perhaps it does not contain sufficient safeguards. I am advancing it by way of amendment in the hope that as a result of further discussion we may bring about a meeting of minds. I hope we may find a way of permitting people to cast their ballots in the way suggested, while at the same time restricting and confining those areas in which abuse might take place.
Briefly, the amendment provides that a person in an urban polling division whose name is not on the voters' list for that polling division may cast his ballot if he takes an oath in which he identifies himself-similar to the oath that is taken in a rural polling division-and if he brings along with him a person, whose name is on the voters' list for that urban polling division and who is a member of a certain occupational or professional group. The occupational or professional groups which would be acceptable in the vouching procedure are those groups which are acceptable to the passport office in cases where the identity of the person must be vouched for in applying for a passport. There are an additional two, or perhaps three, occupational categories which the Canada Elections Act contemplates are composed of people worthy of taking an oath and vouching for a person under the act.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member was kind enough to tell me in a general way of his intention to move this amendment. I therefore had an opportunity of reflecting on the general proposal and looking through this and the consequential amendments. As I indicated on second reading, the Ontario election law provides a certain amount of vouching in urban polls, particularly related to the fact that a person's name may be on a previous municipal list which provides certain evidence of local residence.
I was in favour of the motion as far as extending the privilege to urban voters was concerned. My colleagues have expressed concern. I suppose one's attitude in this regard is dependant upon local experience. I personally have not found any difficulty with the Ontario law, and I find vouching feasible under some circumstances. Some of my colleagues have doubts in this regard. Therefore, I have to approach any voting proposal from the standpoint of whether the concerns expressed to me can be met. I am not satisfied that they can be met by the rather ingenious method employed by the hon. member. He has chosen a rather more limited group than was available, for example, to rural electors.

He is not choosing every elector in the poll but every elector who may come within one of these occupational classes.
There are two difficulties, particularly with reference to his analogy to passport applications. A person attesting to a passport application is required to attest not only as to his knowledge of the individual but to having known the individual for at least two years. In this case there is a situation whereby an individual would present himself to a minister, barrister, dentist, school teacher, bank manager or chartered accountant and say, "I am John Jones. I live at this address, which is in this constituency. I ask you to attest for me in this poll". Unless a person in one of those categories has actual knowledge of the individual's identity and place of residence, if he were a careful person he would say, "You may be both of those things, but how can I be sure? In view of the penalties involved, I do not propose to take that risk". That is what a person in that category would be required to say with regard to a passport application. Unlike normal vouching in a rural case, this is not a case of someone who enjoys propinquity, such as a neighbour or relative. This is a stranger picked from a list. He may not live close to the individual, and for that reason may not be able to attest to his identity and normal residence.
I agree this provision would assist in a limited number of cases where a barrister, bank manager, principal or mayor of the town happened to be a neighbour and could attest to these facts. In a large number of cases that would not apply. The amendment does not get around the basic problem of vouching in urban polls; that is the problem of the anonymity of the city, the fact that people do not necessarily know their neighbours. The difficulty arises when it comes to deciding who should be added to the list, bearing in mind the need to protect the system. My inclination would be to vote against the proposal even though I am concerned that the urban voter is placed at a disadvantage by reason of the absence of the vouching power.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)

I have not had a chance to look at the interesting document I received a short while ago. We are all concerned about the difference between rural and urban voters when an election has been called and constituents have not been properly enumerated.
I notice there are still elements of discrimina-
June 23, 1970

tion here. We are getting used to urban people receiving mail in five days and country people in six, and I am not sure I like that. But in this case only a certain group of urban people can attest, whereas in a rural poll any voter may do so. As my hon. friend, the Rhodes scholar from Edmonton-West, has pointed out, there is even discrimination in the group mentioned here. I greatly resent the suggestion that a barrister is more competent to perform this duty than a university professor. So there are internal problems.
A little more serious is the potential danger that where there is too relaxed an attitude on election day, there might be a corresponding relaxation beforehand of the activity of revising officers, and so on, so that what was gained on election day might be lost in the other stages of the enumeration process. This is the kind of consideration I should like to weigh and reflect on. I should like to consult with the sage of Peace River and others before I would be ready to say this proposal was good. It is too bad that it was not brought up in the committee, where we might have reflected on it during the long nights of the winter.

Had the hon. member had the wisdom to look to the mother of all elections acts in Canada, the province of Nova Scotia, he might have found a precedent for dealing with the urban vote in a more successful way. I, too, wish this matter had been brought up in the committee so we might have given attention to it there.
The principal objection I would have to the proposal is this: In spite of the long list of those eligible for duty, albeit it does not include university professors, it would be difficult on election day to find one of these individuals prepared to do this work, particularly if one did not know a person in one of the categories mentioned. I cannot imagine going to my bank manager and asking him to do something like that for me. I am not saying, of course, that I am not grateful to him; in fact, my bank manager is one of the finest men in Canada.

speechtext: I will make sure he hears about what you have just said.

Canada Elections Act

I might do that. I will take it in when I discuss my overdraft. There is a simple procedure which has been tested in Nova Scotia. In spite of the fears of those responsible for the conduct of elections, it has been found to be highly successful and no abuses were apparent. I suppose some abuses did occur, but my suggestion is that these were negligible in terms of what we are seeking to achieve. What I have in mind is that a procedure might be worked out whereby an elector who found that his name was not included on the list would appear at the poll and then be directed to a place where the returning officer would be sitting. There, he could make his argument and persuade the revising officer to issue a simple certificate which he could then take back to the polling station, accompanied by another elector whose name was on the list and who would be prepared to vouch for him by taking a simple oath.
This is the procedure which has been tested in elections in Nova Scotia and found not wanting. In the urban centres where it has been used, it has restored the right to exercise their franchise to a substantial number of people who would not otherwise have been able to vote. Once an elector has persuaded a revising officer that he is entitled to vote, the procedure is akin to that followed in the rural poll. The difference is, of course, that in a rural poll where there is general knowledge of the people entitled to vote in the area, it is not necessary for a voter to make an appearance at a special sitting of a revising officer or of the returning officer.

I want to say that I regard the policy of the government in this area as utterly reprehensible. To continue to tell us that nothing can be done until we have the white paper on social security is, I think, just stalling for time. In the meantime, we have had changes in some pension legislation, notably the very acceptable improvements in the pensions of retired public servants and improvements in the pensions of Members of Parliament, which some of us did not regard as acceptable.

We have also had the tabling of the white paper on unemployment insurance. We have had the tabling and acceptance by the House, at least so far as concurrence is concerned, of the second report of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. In other words, we are getting bits and pieces of the picture so far as social legislation is concerned. Yet this document, which is supposed to be basic and fundamental to the whole story, is withheld from us. I cannot believe it is withheld because it is impossible to get the document completed, translated or anything like that. It seems to me the situation has all the earmarks of plain stalling because the government does not want to act in this field. In the meantime, our senior citizens are suffering real privation because of the rising cost of living. It has gone up now close to 18 per cent since the present level of the old age pension, plus the guaranteed income supplement, was set. The increase the pensioners have received because of the cost of living increase falls far below the increase that has taken place in the cost of living itself, so that they are being shortchanged about $10 out of every hundred.
What we are getting now, if I may use his own word, is the canard being circulated by the Prime Minister to the effect that it is the workers of this country, especially unionized workers, who are hurting the old age pensioners. He used a certain word most of us recall. I suggest this is a canard which is unworthy of the Prime Minister. It is not good enough to go to the automobile factories and tell the employees they are making life miserable for the senior citizens when it is the failure of this government to take any step in this field which is responsible for the plight of our senior citizens.
Therefore, it seems to me it is a perfectly reasonable request I have been making now for a long time that there should be an interim increase in the amount of the old age pension. I should like to see the legislation completely overhauled. I should like to see a substantial increase in the pension and see the legislation placed on a sound basis. I am prepared to admit that that would take time. In the meantime, however, there could be an increase to, say, $100 a month in the basic pension and a corresponding increase to $40 a month in the guaranteed income supplement. I suggest that nothing less than this is in order at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government shares the very humanitarian feelings expressed by the hon. member. It is easy to go one better in this field, particularly when one does not have the responsibility of governing and implementing the recommendations made to the government.
More than once has the government voiced its interest in senior citizens. About 1,671,000 of them receive the old age pension of $79.58 and 812,000 get the supplement of $31.33, and this is costing the nation $1,730,500,000.
The government has reduced the age for eligibility from 70 to 65, thus increasing the number of recipients by 440,000. It has also granted an increase of 2 per cent to take into account the rise in the cost of living. The universal and contributory pension fund also gives an increasing number of people each year a worthwhile income.
For those who are more especially needy, the central government, because of the new public assistance act, pays 50 per cent of all additional assistance granted by the provinces to aged persons, and 50 per cent of the cost of any additional health and welfare services not covered by hospital insurance and medical insurance plans, and more especially for those who need special at-home care.
Finally, with an across-the-board medicare plan in Canada, the government also pays most medical expenses previously borne by aged persons. All those charges are now met by the state.
We recognize that there is room for improvement, and the government is well aware of it. Thus, the government is pursuing the general review of its entire social security policy. Its conclusions will be published in a white paper, as soon as the study is completed, and it will guide the government's new policy on social security towards the wellbeing of all Canadians, especially the old.
