COMMUNICATION'S-GRANT TO INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS MACHINES TO BUILD ELECTRONIC COMPONENT MANUFACTURING PLANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 9 I addressed the following question to the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans):
In view of the minister's expressed interest in the development of a Canadian controlled computer
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
and communications industry, would the minister inform the House whether he was consulted by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion prior to his announcement of a $6 million grant to International Business Machines Corporation to build an electronic component manufacturing plant in Quebec?
This question is of considerable interest to me because it is a very large grant, some $6 million, and the total estimated capital cost is only $21 million. I understand from information available that this particular plant will provide some 600 to 700 jobs within three years time. This is quite a high average in terms of the amount of money spent per job produced, but in part this is an indication of the type of industry with which we are dealing. We are dealing with one of the de luxe industries of the future, one of the most important industries of the future, when we are considering questions of economic control and economic development.
There are three major questions that need to be considered in connection with this announcement. The first is the question of a Canadian controlled computer industry. I addressed the question to the minister because on a number of occasions he has expressed great interest in the development of a Canadian controlled computer and communications industry. But, on the other hand, we now see a government department providing a very substantial grant to a foreign controlled corporation to build this plant. It seems to me that we have a conflict of policy that must be resolved at once. In addition, this subsidy to a foreign corporation, International Business Machines Corporation, will provide competition for the one Canadian owned plant which is in a similar line of production.
The second matter is the entire question of the problem of foreign ownership. I have raised this matter on a number of occasions in the House in connection with the government's industrial development incentive legislation, because apparently the government is not concerned about the implications of grants which are made to foreign controlled corporations. It apparently is not concerned that these grants will conflict with its policy regarding foreign ownership, which we anticipate some time later this year. Thus, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the government, in the policy it is now following, has not exhibited any will really to come to grips with the problems involved in the high degree of foreign ownership and control which we have in the Canadian economy.
June 23. 1970

The third question that comes to my attention is, why does such a wealthy and prosperous firm, really one of the most prosperous firms on the face of the globe, have to be given a grant? It seems to me if it were felt that a public expenditure of the size that was committed in this case, namely, $6 million to build a plant in this particular location-I am not quarreling with either one of these factors in itself-was justified, then why is there not some public control or ownership of the plant itself? It seems to me that there is a need for public ownership of this plant if we are to ensure that national objectives will be achieved in the future. One of these national objectives is to ensure that there is an adequate degree of development within each of the economic regions in Canada. After all, this is the purpose of the legislation, and of these grants, but there is no guarantee that within the foreseeable future these objectives will be achieved. Once a certain period of time has elapsed, there will be no further control over this plant or its operations.
[DOT] (11:20 p.m.)
It seems to me there is a question of public interest that must be considered, and to date it has not been considered adequately by the government. I would urge the government to re-examine its approach to the industrial development incentive grants now being

As the Minister of Communications said, this is something we need in Canada. It is one of the things that we should be working toward. There are many steps that are necessary if we are to ensure a Canadian identity in the future, so I uge the government to reconsider its position on these scores.
